title: Linguistic drivers of misinformation diffusion on social media during the COVID-19 pandemic
screen_reason: The paper's aim is to model linguistic drivers of retweeting, but in its Empirical analysis section it reports a descriptive share of a defined item sample coded as misinformation: 223 of 1,103 #5G/#Huawei tweets were manually coded as misinformative. That is a quantitative share with a denominator over all items that exist in the sampled corpus, i.e. CONTENT.

estimates.date: Scraped 8 May 2020; tweets from the first week of May 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of #5G/#Huawei tweets manually coded as misinformative
estimates.denominator: 1,103 tweets containing the hashtags #5G and #Huawei scraped on 8 May 2020, after removing verified users and retweets (from 4,923 scraped)
estimates.definition: Tweet manually coded by the three authors as 'related to misinformation' — e.g. claims linking 5G/Huawei to the spread of coronavirus, or asserting 5G is evil/harmful
estimates.misinfo_def: Fake news is defined as news "intentionally and verifiably false and could mislead readers" (Allcott & Gentzkow, 2017, p. 213)
estimates.source_quote: The three authors manually coded the content of tweets, founding that 223 out of 1103 tweets were misinformative
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The three authors each manually coded every tweet as misinformation vs not; near-perfect intercoder agreement reported (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.971). No external fact-check or source list used.
estimates.moderator_quote: we scraped from Twitter 4923 tweets containing the hashtags #5 g #Huawei on May, 8 2020. The dataset was streamlined by removing verified users and retweets. The refined dataset includes 1103 tweets.
estimates.notes: Denominator is the analysed corpus (1,103), not the 4,923 originally scraped, because coding was done on the refined set. Corpus is a two-hashtag single-issue keyword capture (the 5G/Huawei–coronavirus conspiracy), so denom_scope=topical with no curation. Topic coded covid19 because the misinformation at issue is the 5G–coronavirus conspiracy during the pandemic, though the hashtags are technology/brand terms. Verified users were excluded from the corpus, which will bias the share relative to all #5G/#Huawei tweets.

missed_or_uncertain: Table 1 gives LIWC descriptive statistics split by Fake/Nofake but those are scale means of linguistic variables, not prevalence shares — no rows. The logit/Poisson coefficients (Tables 2–3) and the gradient-boosting classification accuracies (83.92%, 98.93% of negatives, 0.74% of positives; xgboost 83.58%/96.93%/9.63%; logit 83.24%/97.32%/5.19%) are model-performance figures, not misinformation prevalence — excluded. 175 of 1,103 tweets were retweeted, but the paper does not report the share of retweets that carried misinformation, so no SHARING row is derivable (a cross-tabulation would have to be computed, which R8 forbids).

rob.design: Convenience keyword capture of 4,923 tweets carrying #5G and #Huawei on 8 May 2020; verified users and retweets removed leaving 1,103 tweets. All three authors hand-coded every tweet for misinformation, Krippendorff's alpha = 0.971. No sampling weights, no response rate (non-survey), no external ground truth; single one-week window, English-language hashtags, country not reported.
rob.item6_quote: Fake news is defined as news "intentionally and verifiably false and could mislead readers" (Allcott & Gentzkow, 2017, p. 213).
rob.item10_quote: The three authors manually coded the content of tweets, founding that 223 out of 1103 tweets were misinformative, reaching a near-perfect degree of agreement (Krippendorff α=0.971).
